# T16 - Representation Closure and Open Intelligence

**Residual Boundaries, Attention, and Governed Completion in Learned Systems**

**Leonardo Murillo Montero**

*First draft - May 26, 2026*

---

> *Intelligence completes boundaries; aligned intelligence governs completion.*

---

## Abstract

**Situation.** T13 proved that projection creates boundary sources and that finite renormalization is the closure operator generated by conductor fusion. T14 proved that curvature, renormalization source, beta flow, and Noether defect are the same projection-boundary obstruction. T15 proved that continuum completion is a fixed point of refinement, fusion closure, and real-place boundary inclusion. These results turn "residual" from an error word into a structural word.

**Gap.** Modern AI systems are built from projections: embeddings, activations, attention heads, sparse features, residual streams, retrieval, tools, memory, and user feedback. Current language treats hallucination, shortcut learning, out-of-distribution failure, attention routing, tool use, interpretability, and alignment as separate problems. The lamed-series suggests a single mechanism: a model chooses a retained representation sector; if that sector is not closed under task interactions, missing boundaries return as residual behavior.

**Action.** We prove fifteen structure theorems. First, the **Feature Sector Theorem**: a learned representation is a retained observable sector or finite coordinate algebra. Second, the **Representation Boundary Theorem**: residuals decompose into structural boundary plus statistical, optimization, and noise terms. Third, the **Layerwise Closure Flow Theorem**: depth implements capacity-constrained boundary adjunction. Fourth, the **Attention as Boundary Router Theorem**: attention dynamically chooses which boundary interactions are admitted at a token/location. Fifth, the **Residual Stream Conservation Theorem**: residual connections implement extensivity of closure flow. Sixth, the **Sparse Autoencoder Certificate Theorem**: SAE residuals can certify missing boundary directions. Seventh, the **Shortcut Blind-Spot Theorem**: shortcuts are nonclosed sectors whose boundary is hidden by training support. Eighth, the **Label Smoothing / Regularization Boundary Theorem**: regularization helps when it damps unresolved boundary modes. Ninth, the **Capacity Bound / Closure Budget Theorem**: exact closure requires enough capacity to represent the closure. Tenth, the **Tool and Memory as Archimedean Boundary Theorem**: tools, retrieval, memory, environment interaction, and user feedback supply open-world boundary completion. Eleventh, the **Representation Completion Fixed-Point Theorem**: cognition seeks task-relative completion fixed points. Twelfth, the **Architecture of Intelligence Theorem**: robust intelligence requires the operations that form, detect, route, certify, compress, and stabilize boundaries. Thirteenth, the **Boundary-Stable Generalization Theorem**: generalization is stability of unresolved boundaries under support shift. Fourteenth, the **Alignment as Boundary Governance Theorem**: alignment is lawful routing of boundary completion. Fifteenth, the **Governed Open Completion Theorem**: robust intelligence is boundary-stable governed completion under capacity.

**Result.** The central compression is
\[
\boxed{
\text{intelligence}
=
\text{boundary-aware completion under capacity},
\qquad
\text{alignment}
=
\text{boundary governance}.
}
\]
Generalization is not merely interpolation. It is boundary stability as the world changes.

**Harvest.** T16 turns the previous finite mathematics into an AI architecture theorem. Learned systems are not neutral encoders. They are projection-completion machines. The central practical question becomes: what boundary is the model trying to complete, does it have the capacity to complete it, and is it allowed to complete it that way?

**Keywords:** representation closure, AI architecture, residual boundary, attention, sparse autoencoders, shortcut learning, label smoothing, tool use, memory, open-world completion, generalization, alignment, boundary governance, capacity, fixed point.

## Notation

Let \(\Omega\) be a finite data/state space. The full real observable algebra is
\[
\mathbb R^\Omega=\{f:\Omega\to\mathbb R\}.
\]

A learned representation is a map
\[
Y_S:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m,
\qquad
Y_S=(Y_{S,1},\ldots,Y_{S,m}).
\]
Its retained linear feature sector is
\[
H_S=\operatorname{span}\{Y_{S,1},\ldots,Y_{S,m}\}\subseteq\mathbb R^\Omega.
\]
Its finite coordinate algebra is
\[
A_S=\mathbb R[z_1,\ldots,z_m]/I(Y_S(\Omega)),
\]
where
\[
I(Y_S(\Omega))
=
\{f\in\mathbb R[z_1,\ldots,z_m]: f(v)=0\text{ for all }v\in Y_S(\Omega)\}.
\]

Let
\[
V_n:H^{\otimes n}\to H
\]
be a task interaction: a product, attention interaction, cumulant vertex, compositional feature operation, or other task-relevant multilinear/nonlinear interaction after linearization in an appropriate feature algebra.

Let \(\Pi_S\) be projection onto the retained sector \(H_S\), and \(\Pi_0\) projection onto a declared trivial/gauge/constant sector. The structural boundary of \(S\) under \(V_n\) is represented by
\[
(1-\Pi_S-\Pi_0)V_n(H_S,\ldots,H_S).
\]
We write its support as \(\partial_nS\) or \(\partial_{\mathcal T}S\) when the task/environment class \(\mathcal T\) is emphasized.

Let \(C\) be a capacity budget. Let \(\mathcal K_C\) denote capacity-constrained compression/selection. Let \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal T}\) denote external boundary routing by tools, retrieval, memory, environment interaction, or user feedback. Let \(\mathcal G\) be a governance specification.

The governed representation completion operator is
\[
\widehat S_{\mathcal G,C}
=
\mathcal G\circ
\mathcal E_{\mathcal T}\circ
\mathcal K_C\circ
\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathcal T}(S).
\]

## 1. Why intelligence is open completion

The previous papers developed a repeated pattern:
\[
\text{projection}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{boundary}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{closure or completion}.
\]
In AI, this is not abstract ornament. A learned model is made from projections. It compresses a world into features. Those features are not neutral. They decide what the model can currently see, combine, remember, route, certify, and govern.

When a retained representation sector is closed under the task interactions, residuals are ordinary statistical and noise terms. When it is not closed, the missing boundary returns as systematic behavior: hallucination, shortcut learning, brittle generalization, overconfident extrapolation, tool misuse, or unsafe completion.

T16 therefore treats intelligence as the architecture of boundary management:
\[
\boxed{
\text{form sectors, detect boundaries, route them, compress them, certify them, complete them, govern them}.
}
\]

---

## 2. Feature sectors

### Theorem 1. Feature Sector Theorem

Let
\[
Y_S:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m
\]
be a learned representation. Then \(Y_S\) determines a retained observable sector
\[
H_S=\operatorname{span}\{Y_{S,1},\ldots,Y_{S,m}\}\subseteq\mathbb R^\Omega.
\]
Equivalently, \(Y_S\) determines the finite coordinate algebra
\[
A_S=\mathbb R[z_1,\ldots,z_m]/I(Y_S(\Omega)).
\]
Thus a learned representation is not a neutral encoding. It is a projection or quotient of the full observable algebra.

**Proof.** Since \(\Omega\) is finite, every coordinate
\[
Y_{S,j}:\Omega\to\mathbb R
\]
is an observable. Their span is a subspace of the full observable space:
\[
H_S\subseteq\mathbb R^\Omega.
\]

For the algebraic form, define
\[
\Phi_S:\mathbb R[z_1,\ldots,z_m]\to\mathbb R^\Omega,
\qquad
\Phi_S(f)=f\circ Y_S.
\]
This is an algebra homomorphism. Its kernel is exactly the ideal of polynomials vanishing on the finite representation image:
\[
\ker\Phi_S=I(Y_S(\Omega)).
\]
By the first isomorphism theorem,
\[
\operatorname{im}\Phi_S
\cong
\mathbb R[z_1,\ldots,z_m]/I(Y_S(\Omega)).
\]
Therefore \(A_S\) is precisely the algebra of observables visible through \(Y_S\). Embeddings, activations, SAE features, attention-head outputs, and residual-stream coordinates are different coordinate choices on such retained sectors. \(\square\)

---

## 3. Representation boundaries

### Theorem 2. Representation Boundary Theorem

Let \(H_S\subseteq H\) be a retained feature sector, and let \(V_n\) be a task interaction. The residual of the best retained representation decomposes as
\[
\mathrm{Res}_S
=
\Pi_{\partial_nS}V_n
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stat}}
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}.
\]
The boundary term
\[
\Pi_{\partial_nS}V_n
\]
is structural: it vanishes for all retained inputs if and only if \(H_S\) is closed under \(V_n\) up to trivial modes.

**Proof.** The task interaction produces
\[
V_n(u_1,\ldots,u_n),
\qquad u_i\in H_S.
\]
The best representable retained component is
\[
\Pi_SV_n(u_1,\ldots,u_n).
\]
The nontrivial part outside the retained sector is
\[
(1-\Pi_S-\Pi_0)V_n(u_1,\ldots,u_n).
\]
This is the structural boundary term \(\Pi_{\partial_nS}V_n\).

Empirical residuals also contain finite-sample error, optimization error, and noise. Hence
\[
\mathrm{Res}_S
=
\Pi_{\partial_nS}V_n
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stat}}
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}.
\]

The structural term vanishes for all retained inputs exactly when
\[
V_n(H_S,\ldots,H_S)\subseteq H_S\oplus H_0.
\]
That is closure under the task interaction up to trivial modes. If closure fails, no model restricted to \(H_S\) can represent the missing component as an element of \(H_S\). \(\square\)

---

## 4. Layerwise closure

### Theorem 3. Layerwise Closure Flow Theorem

Let a depth-\(L\) network define representations
\[
Y_\ell:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{m_\ell},
\qquad
\ell=0,\ldots,L,
\]
with retained sectors \(H_{S_\ell}\). Assume each layer has the form
\[
Y_{\ell+1}=R_\ell Y_\ell+B_\ell(Y_\ell),
\]
where \(R_\ell\) transports old information and \(B_\ell\) is a learned block such as attention, MLP, convolution, or adapter. Then each layer implements an approximate capacity-constrained closure step
\[
S_{\ell+1}\subseteq\operatorname{Cl}_{n,\mathcal C_\ell}(S_\ell),
\]
where \(\mathcal C_\ell\) is the layer capacity constraint. Thus depth implements finite RG under capacity.

**Proof.** By Theorem 1, \(Y_\ell\) defines \(H_{S_\ell}\). By Theorem 2, \(V_n\) produces a boundary
\[
(1-\Pi_{S_\ell}-\Pi_0)V_n(H_{S_\ell},\ldots,H_{S_\ell})
\]
with support \(\partial_nS_\ell\).

The next layer cannot adjoin arbitrary observables. It is restricted by width, rank, sparsity, attention pattern, parameter budget, and optimization. Collect these restrictions as \(\mathcal C_\ell\), and define \(\operatorname{Cl}_{n,\mathcal C_\ell}(S_\ell)\) as the admissible closure step obtained by adjoining, suppressing, compressing, or rerouting the allowed part of \(\partial_nS_\ell\).

The residual/transport term \(R_\ell Y_\ell\) carries old sector information forward, while \(B_\ell(Y_\ell)\) can only build new observables from current features and their allowed interactions. Therefore the next sector lies inside the capacity-constrained closure:
\[
S_{\ell+1}\subseteq\operatorname{Cl}_{n,\mathcal C_\ell}(S_\ell).
\]
Iterating gives a closure flow
\[
S_0\to S_1\to\cdots\to S_L.
\]
\(\square\)

---

## 5. Attention as boundary routing

### Theorem 4. Attention as Boundary Router Theorem

Let \(H_S\) be the current retained feature sector at a token/location \(x\). Let \(\mathcal P_x\) be the admissible family of attention routing operators. For each \(\Pi\in\mathcal P_x\), define
\[
\partial_\Pi S=(1-\Pi-\Pi_0)V_n(H_S,\ldots,H_S).
\]
If the trained attention block optimizes an effective objective
\[
\mathcal J_x(\Pi)
=
\mathcal L_x(\Pi)
+
\lambda\|\partial_\Pi S\|
+
\mu\,\mathrm{FrameCost}(\Pi),
\]
then ideally
\[
\mathrm{Attn}(x)
=
\arg\min_{\Pi\in\mathcal P_x}\mathcal J_x(\Pi),
\]
and trained finite models approximate this. Thus attention is dynamic projection control: it conditionally routes which boundary interactions are admitted.

**Proof.** An attention head computes weights
\[
\alpha_i(x)=\frac{\exp(q(x)\cdot k_i)}{\sum_j\exp(q(x)\cdot k_j)}
\]
and returns
\[
\sum_i\alpha_i(x)v_i.
\]
This is a context-dependent routing operator, denoted \(\Pi_x\), from available value directions into the next representation.

For a routing choice \(\Pi\), the admitted part of a task interaction is
\[
\Pi V_n(H_S,\ldots,H_S),
\]
and the unresolved part is
\[
(1-\Pi-\Pi_0)V_n(H_S,\ldots,H_S)=\partial_\Pi S.
\]
If training effectively penalizes prediction loss, unresolved boundary mass, and frame cost, then the ideal optimizer is the stated argmin. Since \(\Pi_x\) depends on token/location through the query, attention dynamically changes which boundary is routed. \(\square\)

---

## 6. Residual stream conservation

### Theorem 5. Residual Stream Conservation Theorem

Let
\[
Y_{\ell+1}=T_\ell Y_\ell+B_\ell(Y_\ell),
\]
where \(T_\ell\) is an injective transport of the old representation and \(B_\ell\) is a boundary-correction block. Then, up to change of coordinates,
\[
H_{S_\ell}\subseteq H_{S_{\ell+1}}.
\]
Residual streams implement the extensivity axiom of closure flow:
\[
S_\ell\subseteq S_{\ell+1}.
\]

**Proof.** Since \(T_\ell\) is injective, the image \(T_\ell H_{S_\ell}\) is isomorphic to \(H_{S_\ell}\). The next representation contains the transported old features plus the new features produced by \(B_\ell\):
\[
H_{S_{\ell+1}}\supseteq T_\ell H_{S_\ell}.
\]
Identifying \(H_{S_\ell}\) with its transported copy gives
\[
H_{S_\ell}\subseteq H_{S_{\ell+1}}.
\]
This is exactly extensivity:
\[
S\subseteq\operatorname{Cl}(S).
\]
Without a residual transport, a layer could replace old sector data by a non-injective transformation, breaking monotone closure flow. \(\square\)

---

## 7. Sparse autoencoder certificates

### Theorem 6. Sparse Autoencoder Certificate Theorem

Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be an activation space, and let an SAE learn a dictionary
\[
D=\{d_1,\ldots,d_m\}
\]
with projection
\[
\Pi_S:A\to \hat H_S=\operatorname{span}(D).
\]
If the dictionary resolves the retained feature sector, then missing boundary packets are detectable by
\[
\widehat{\partial_nS}
=
\operatorname{support}\big((1-\Pi_S)V_n(\hat H_S^{\otimes n})\big).
\]
Systematic nonzero support certifies missing boundary directions.

**Proof.** The SAE decoder dictionary defines the empirical retained sector
\[
\hat H_S=\operatorname{span}(D).
\]
The encoder-decoder map acts as a projection \(\Pi_S\) onto that sector. If the SAE resolves \(S\), retained activations reconstruct to small error:
\[
a\approx\Pi_Sa.
\]

If \(V_n\) maps interactions of retained SAE features back into \(\hat H_S\), then
\[
(1-\Pi_S)V_n(\hat H_S^{\otimes n})=0.
\]
If this quantity is systematically nonzero, retained features interact to produce activation directions not represented by the dictionary. Their support is the empirical boundary certificate
\[
\widehat{\partial_nS}.
\]
Thus SAEs can test closure: reconstruct, interact, project back, and measure the unexplained support. \(\square\)

---

## 8. Shortcut blind spots

### Theorem 7. Shortcut Blind-Spot Theorem

Let \(T:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) be a target, with training distribution \(\mu_{\mathrm{train}}\) and deployment distribution \(\mu_{\mathrm{test}}\). Suppose a low-cost nonclosed sector \(H_{S'}\) contains a predictor \(f_{S'}\) satisfying
\[
T=f_{S'}
\qquad
\mu_{\mathrm{train}}\text{-a.e.}
\]
but its boundary is hidden on training support and visible on deployment support:
\[
\Pi_{\partial_nS'}V_n=0
\quad \mu_{\mathrm{train}}\text{-a.e.},
\]
\[
\Pi_{\partial_nS'}V_n\ne0
\quad \mu_{\mathrm{test}}\text{ on a set of positive measure}.
\]
Then \(f_{S'}\) is a shortcut. Generalization failure is boundary exposure.

**Proof.** The equality \(T=f_{S'}\) on training support gives zero ideal population training error. Since the boundary vanishes on that support, training data cannot distinguish \(S'\) from a closed sector.

But \(H_{S'}\) is not closed under \(V_n\). By Theorem 2, the residual contains the structural boundary \(\Pi_{\partial_nS'}V_n\). On deployment support this boundary is nonzero on a set of positive measure, so the test error contains a nonzero structural contribution:
\[
\|\Pi_{\partial_nS'}V_n\|_{L^2(\mu_{\mathrm{test}})}^2>0
\]
up to ordinary error terms. This cannot be removed by further training restricted to \(H_{S'}\). The shortcut succeeded only because the training distribution hid the boundary. \(\square\)

---

## 9. Regularization as boundary damping

### Theorem 8. Label Smoothing / Regularization Boundary Theorem

Let \(G=\mathbb Z/N\), let \(u\) be uniform, and write
\[
p=u+r,
\qquad
\sum_sr_s=0.
\]
For label smoothing
\[
p^\alpha=(1-\alpha)p+\alpha u,
\qquad 0\le\alpha\le1,
\]
all nontrivial conductor packets are damped:
\[
\Pi_d(p^\alpha-u)=(1-\alpha)\Pi_d(p-u),
\qquad d>1.
\]
If an \(n\)-leg boundary curvature term is multilinear in nontrivial retained components, then
\[
\|\partial_nS(p^\alpha)\|
\le
(1-\alpha)^n\|\partial_nS(p)\|.
\]
Thus regularization improves generalization when it reduces unresolved boundary modes.

**Proof.** Since
\[
p^\alpha-u=(1-\alpha)(p-u)=(1-\alpha)r,
\]
and \(u\) lies in the trivial packet, every nontrivial packet projection satisfies
\[
\Pi_d(p^\alpha-u)=(1-\alpha)\Pi_d(p-u).
\]
Thus nontrivial packet energies scale by \((1-\alpha)^2\).

If \(\partial_nS\) is produced by an \(n\)-linear interaction of nontrivial retained components, then multilinearity gives
\[
\partial_nS(p^\alpha)=(1-\alpha)^n\partial_nS(p).
\]
Taking norms yields the bound. More general regularizers help when they penalize packet energy, boundary norm, or projected curvature defect, thereby pushing the model toward smoother closure-compatible sectors. \(\square\)

---

## 10. Capacity budgets

### Theorem 9. Capacity Bound / Closure Budget Theorem

Let \(S\) be a retained feature sector, and let \(\operatorname{Cl}_n(S)\) be its closure under \(V_n\). Let \(C\) be model capacity and let \(C_{\min}(\operatorname{Cl}_n(S))\) be the minimum capacity required to represent the full closure without loss. Exact internal closure is possible only if
\[
C\ge C_{\min}(\operatorname{Cl}_n(S)).
\]
If
\[
C<C_{\min}(\operatorname{Cl}_n(S)),
\]
the model must compress, route externally, ignore, or approximate/hallucinate the boundary.

**Proof.** By definition, \(\operatorname{Cl}_n(S)\) is the smallest sector containing \(S\) closed under \(V_n\). Any exact internal closed representation containing \(S\) must represent all components of \(\operatorname{Cl}_n(S)\). If capacity \(C\) is below the minimum required to represent that sector, exact internal closure would contradict the definition of \(C_{\min}\).

Thus exact internal closure requires the stated inequality. Below the threshold, a forced boundary component cannot all be represented internally. It must therefore be compressed, routed externally, discarded, or approximated by lower-cost correlates. These alternatives exhaust the possibilities. \(\square\)

---

## 11. Tools and memory as open boundary

### Theorem 10. Tool and Memory as Archimedean Boundary Theorem

Let a finite model have internal retained sector \(H_S\) and internal closure \(\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathrm{int}}(S)\). Let \(H_{\mathcal T}\) be the observable sector required by an open-world task/environment class \(\mathcal T\). If
\[
H_{\mathcal T}\nsubseteq\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathrm{int}}(S),
\]
then the model has an open-world boundary
\[
\partial_{\mathrm{open}}S
=
H_{\mathcal T}/\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathrm{int}}(S).
\]
Tools, retrieval, memory, environment interaction, and user feedback are external boundary maps whose image supplies missing components. A tool-using model forms
\[
\widehat H_S
=
\operatorname{Cl}(H_S+\operatorname{im}E).
\]
When \(\partial_{\mathrm{open}}S\subseteq\operatorname{im}E\) up to task tolerance, external routing completes the model relative to \(\mathcal T\).

**Proof.** A finite model can only internally represent \(\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathrm{int}}(S)\). Open-world tasks may require current facts, private documents, computations, environment state, user intent, or data not present in parameters. These live in \(H_{\mathcal T}\). If \(H_{\mathcal T}\) is not contained in the internal closure, the quotient is an unresolved open boundary.

External systems implement maps
\[
E:H_{\mathrm{query}}\to H_{\mathrm{ext}}.
\]
Their returned information enlarges the effective sector:
\[
H_S\mapsto H_S+\operatorname{im}E.
\]
Closing under task interactions gives
\[
\widehat H_S=\operatorname{Cl}(H_S+\operatorname{im}E).
\]
If the missing boundary is included in \(\operatorname{im}E\) within tolerance, the externally completed system can represent what the finite internal model could not. This is the AI analog of T15's real-place boundary: finite internal closure plus terminal external completion. \(\square\)

---

## 12. Completion fixed points

### Theorem 11. Representation Completion Fixed-Point Theorem

Fix a task/environment class \(\mathcal T\). Define
\[
\widehat S
=
\mathcal E_{\mathcal T}\big(\mathcal K_C(\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathcal T}(S))\big),
\]
where \(\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathcal T}\) closes under task interactions, \(\mathcal K_C\) compresses under capacity, and \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal T}\) routes external boundary information. Then \(S\) is complete relative to \(\mathcal T\) if and only if
\[
\widehat S=S.
\]
An intelligent architecture implements an iterative process
\[
S_{k+1}\approx\widehat S_k
\]
whose goal is to approach such fixed points.

**Proof.** If \(\widehat S=S\), then task closure, capacity compression, and external routing add no new effective representational content. Thus \(S\) is complete relative to \(\mathcal T\).

Conversely, if \(S\) is complete relative to \(\mathcal T\), task closure adds nothing required, compression does not discard required content, and external routing finds no unresolved missing boundary beyond the completed sector. Therefore applying \(\widehat{(\cdot)}\) returns \(S\).

Networks, agents, retrieval systems, and feedback loops update representations iteratively. When unresolved boundary decreases and stabilizes, the sequence approaches a fixed point. \(\square\)

---

## 13. Architecture of intelligence

### Theorem 12. Architecture of Intelligence Theorem

Fix a task/environment class \(\mathcal T\). Define a learned system to be task-intelligent when it can iteratively reduce unresolved representation boundary and approach a task-relative completion fixed point. Then a learned system is intelligent on \(\mathcal T\) only if it supports:

1. feature sector formation;
2. boundary detection;
3. layerwise closure flow;
4. dynamic attention routing;
5. residual extensivity;
6. sparse/probe certification;
7. shortcut boundary control;
8. capacity-aware compression;
9. external/open-world completion;
10. fixed-point stabilization.

Conversely, a system supporting these operations has the formal architecture required to implement task-relative representation completion.

**Proof.** By Theorem 11, task-relative completion is governed by
\[
\widehat S
=
\mathcal E_{\mathcal T}
\big(\mathcal K_C(\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathcal T}(S))\big).
\]
Without feature sectors there is no \(S\). Without boundary detection the system cannot distinguish structural residual from noise. Without layerwise closure it cannot adjoin missing interactions. Without attention routing it cannot choose local boundary terms. Without residual extensivity it can destroy prior sectors while updating. Without probes it cannot certify closure. Without shortcut control it can hide nonclosure behind training support. Without capacity-aware compression it cannot manage the case \(C<C_{\min}\). Without external completion it cannot close open-world tasks. Without fixed-point stabilization it never reaches a task-relative completed state.

Thus the operations are necessary. If the system supports them, it can form \(S_0\), detect and route boundaries, preserve prior information, certify missing features, avoid shortcut exposure, compress under capacity, route open boundaries externally, and iterate until
\[
d(S_k,\widehat S_k)\le\varepsilon.
\]
That is approximate task-relative completion. \(\square\)

---

## 14. Boundary-stable generalization

### Theorem 13. Boundary-Stable Generalization Theorem

Let \(S\) be a learned representation sector for \(\mathcal T\), and let \(\mu_{\mathrm{train}}\), \(\mu_{\mathrm{test}}\) be training and deployment distributions. Let the residual decompose as
\[
\mathrm{Res}_S
=
B_S
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stat}}
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}
+
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}},
\]
where
\[
B_S=\Pi_{\partial_{\mathcal T}S}V_{\mathcal T}
\]
is the structural task boundary. Then
\[
\mathcal E_{\mathrm{test}}-\mathcal E_{\mathrm{train}}
=
\left(
\|B_S\|_{\mu_{\mathrm{test}}}^2
-
\|B_S\|_{\mu_{\mathrm{train}}}^2
\right)
+
\Delta_{\mathrm{stat}}
+
\Delta_{\mathrm{opt}}
+
\Delta_{\mathrm{noise}}
+
\Delta_{\mathrm{cross}}.
\]
If ordinary terms are controlled, generalization is governed by boundary stability:
\[
\|B_S\|_{\mu_{\mathrm{test}}}
\approx
\|B_S\|_{\mu_{\mathrm{train}}}.
\]

**Proof.** Write the pointwise residual as
\[
r_S=B_S+e_{\mathrm{stat}}+e_{\mathrm{opt}}+e_{\mathrm{noise}}.
\]
For any distribution \(\mu\),
\[
\mathcal E_\mu=\|r_S\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2.
\]
Expanding the square gives the norm of \(B_S\), the norms of ordinary error terms, and all cross terms. Applying this expansion to \(\mu_{\mathrm{test}}\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{train}}\), then subtracting, yields the displayed decomposition.

When statistical, optimization, noise, and cross-term shifts are controlled, the excess error is dominated by the change in boundary norm. If \(B_S=0\) or is stable, compressed, certified, or routed externally by \(\widehat S\), the model generalizes across the shift. If \(B_S\) was hidden on training support and visible on deployment support, shortcut failure occurs. \(\square\)

---

## 15. Alignment as boundary governance

### Theorem 14. Alignment as Boundary Governance Theorem

Let \(S\) be a model representation sector for \(\mathcal T\), with unresolved boundary \(\partial_{\mathcal T}S\). Let a governance specification \(\mathcal G\) partition boundary components into routing classes:
\[
\partial_{\mathcal T}S
=
\partial_{\mathrm{internal}}
\cup
\partial_{\mathrm{tool}}
\cup
\partial_{\mathrm{user}}
\cup
\partial_{\mathrm{refuse}}
\cup
\partial_{\mathrm{unknown}}.
\]
Let \(\widehat S\) be unconstrained completion and \(\widehat S_{\mathcal G}\) governance-constrained completion. The model is aligned relative to \((\mathcal T,\mathcal G)\) if and only if every boundary component is routed through an allowed channel:
\[
\widehat S_{\mathcal G}=\mathcal G\circ\widehat S.
\]

**Proof.** Unconstrained completion asks what boundary the model would close for task success:
\[
\widehat S
=
\mathcal E_{\mathcal T}\big(\mathcal K_C(\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathcal T}(S))\big).
\]
Alignment asks which closures are permitted and through which channels. The governance specification assigns components to internal closure, tool verification, user clarification, refusal/containment, or uncertainty tracking.

If the model is aligned, its effective completion is the unconstrained completion filtered through \(\mathcal G\):
\[
\widehat S_{\mathcal G}=\mathcal G\circ\widehat S.
\]
Conversely, if this equality holds, no disallowed component is internally completed, no unknown boundary is treated as closed, no underspecified boundary is guessed, and no tool-required boundary is answered without the required route. That is alignment relative to \((\mathcal T,\mathcal G)\). \(\square\)

---

## 16. Governed open completion

### Theorem 15. The Governed Open Completion Theorem

Let \(\mathcal T\) be a task/environment class, \(C\) a capacity budget, and \(\mathcal G\) a governance specification. Define
\[
\widehat S_{\mathcal G,C}
=
\mathcal G\circ
\mathcal E_{\mathcal T}\circ
\mathcal K_C\circ
\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathcal T}(S).
\]
A learned system is robustly intelligent relative to \((\mathcal T,C,\mathcal G)\) if and only if it can iteratively approach boundary-stable governed fixed points
\[
S^*=\widehat S_{\mathcal G,C}(S^*)
\]
while maintaining boundary stability under deployment shifts.

Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\text{robust intelligence}
=
\text{boundary-stable governed completion under capacity}.
}
\]

**Proof.** The operator \(\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathcal T}\) adjoins task-interaction consequences. The operator \(\mathcal K_C\) compresses/selects under finite capacity. The operator \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal T}\) routes open-world boundary through tools, memory, retrieval, environment, or user feedback. The governance map \(\mathcal G\) restricts which completions are allowed.

If a system is robustly intelligent relative to \((\mathcal T,C,\mathcal G)\), it must be able to form feature sectors, detect and route boundaries, preserve old sector data, certify missing features, avoid shortcut exposure, compress under capacity, use external boundary routes, govern completion, and generalize under deployment shifts. By Theorems 1-14, these are precisely the requirements for approaching a fixed point of \(\widehat S_{\mathcal G,C}\) whose unresolved boundary remains stable across the relevant support changes. Thus robust intelligence implies convergence toward such fixed points.

Conversely, suppose a system can iteratively approach fixed points
\[
S^*=\widehat S_{\mathcal G,C}(S^*)
\]
and maintain boundary stability under deployment shifts. Then task closure adds no unresolved internal interaction boundary, capacity compression has selected a feasible representation, external routing supplies open-world missing components, governance prevents disallowed completion routes, and boundary stability controls generalization. By Theorem 12, the system has the formal architecture of intelligence; by Theorem 13, it generalizes through boundary stability; by Theorem 14, it is aligned through boundary governance. Therefore it is robustly intelligent relative to \((\mathcal T,C,\mathcal G)\).

\(\square\)

---

## 17. What T16 does not claim

1. **It does not claim current neural networks literally expose conductor packets.** The conductor-packet language is the structured finite case. General learned systems use feature sectors and coordinate algebras as the broader abstraction.

2. **It does not say all residuals are structural.** Residuals also include statistical, optimization, and noise terms. The claim is that structural boundary is a distinct component that should not be confused with those terms.

3. **It does not make tool use automatically safe.** Tools route open boundaries. Governance decides when and how such routing is allowed.

4. **It does not solve alignment by definition.** It gives a mathematical grammar: alignment is boundary governance. Concrete governance specifications remain substantive human, legal, and institutional work.

5. **It does not replace empirical evaluation.** It predicts what to measure: unresolved boundary, boundary stability, shortcut exposure, certificate support, and routing correctness.

6. **It does not collapse AI into pure math.** It proposes a floor: a structural account of why architectures need residual streams, attention, probes, regularization, tools, memory, and governance.

---

## 18. Forward doors

### 18.1 Boundary metrics for model evaluation

Define empirical norms for \(\partial_{\mathcal T}S\), boundary stability under shifts, and governance routing errors. This gives a new evaluation layer beyond raw accuracy.

### 18.2 SAE-based closure audits

Use sparse autoencoders to estimate \(\widehat{\partial_nS}\) layer by layer and test whether boundary directions are later represented, suppressed, or routed.

### 18.3 Attention routing certificates

Measure whether attention heads route predicted boundary components or merely correlate with surface tokens.

### 18.4 Tool-use governance diagrams

Represent each tool/memory/retrieval call as a boundary route and audit whether the route was allowed by \(\mathcal G\).

### 18.5 Open-world fixed-point agents

Study agents as iterative governed completion systems:
\[
S_0\to \widehat S_{\mathcal G,C}(S_0)\to\widehat S_{\mathcal G,C}^2(S_0)\to\cdots.
\]

---

## 19. Coda

The path from T13 to T16 is:
\[
\text{renormalization is closure},
\]
\[
\text{curvature is projected nonclosure},
\]
\[
\text{continuum is archimedean fixed-point completion},
\]
\[
\text{intelligence is governed open completion}.
\]

The final compression is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{A system is robustly intelligent when it can complete what it knows, route what it lacks, govern what it must not complete, and remain stable when the world changes.}
}
\]
